Decision Time In Vancouver. The Perfect Opportunity. Health Canada Still Has Not Adequately Provided Medical Cannabis. Following Dutch Success or American Failure?

After saying both publicly and privately that they did not have the resources to close Da Kine Smoke and Beverage, the Vancouver Police raided the cannabis shop yesterday evening with a massive show of force.

A dozen or so narks with their guns drawn and wearing balaclava masks charged into Da Kine around six o’clock. They were backed-up on the street by dozens of uniformed police, who turned out to be needed for crowd control. I counted more than ten squad cars, five or so unmarked cars, two paddy wagons, four motor cycles, traffic wardens, and other city staffers.

In the process, they closed down a block of busy Commercial Drive for about four hours. Closing the street had the effect of shutting down a major part of the east side’s electric bus system at the evening rush hour when people are coming home from work. It also closed all of the other businesses on the long block, and delayed a major movie shoot, at enormous cost to the producers – and to Vancouver’s reputation as a good place to do location shoots.

These ferocious drug warriors succeeded in arresting Da Kine owner Carol Gwilt, and five other members of her staff. (None of the clients were arrested.) T’was a great victory. Yeah.

Things started going badly for the narks almost immediately. A very hostile crowd quickly gathered, jeering the police and openly smoking cannabis, even while the police videotaped them – and were taped and photographed in turn by the people.

The Vancouver Sun, whose inflammatory reporting probably helped egg the police into going over the top, reported that the crowd cheered and sang along as a store across the street started playing Bob Marley very loudly. (“I shot the sheriff” cannot be the sort of background music that narks enjoy.)

What is going on here?

The raid was a bit of surprise because the police had repeatedly said that they were going to leave it up to the City Council to decide, but the dramatic nature of the raid was really shocking in the Vancouver context. There is speculation that the raid was so overdone precisely to make cannabis prohibition look both stupid and futile. If that was not the plan, it still succeeded in doing just that.

But it did not succeed in closing Da Kine!

It reopened this morning with a huge media presence and large crowds of supporters on the street. People were honking and cheering as they went by.

This afternoon, Carol and her staff were released without bail, subject only to the requirement that they not go any place where cannabis is being sold. (Many Americans will probably need smelling salts after reading that.)

The next court date will be on October 6th, which is also the new date for the City Council committee hearing on the Da Kine business license. In the meantime, the rest of the staff plan on business as usual. It remains to be seen what the police will do in the face of such open defiance. Today, there was one squad car parked at the end of the block, but so-far-so-good… Stay tuned.

Your Reporter Saved By Mexican Food.

I went to Da Kine late yesterday afternoon to talk to Carol. After a brief conversation, I concluded that they were so busy that I should come back a little later, so I went up the street to my favorite Mexican food restaurant (Tio Pepe’s).

When I came out, about 30 minutes later, the street was closed and the narks were jammed into Da Kine. I walked around the perimeter for a while, and concluded that I am getting a bit too old for that sort of thing and went home and went to bed. It had been an “interesting” day.

The Kubbys homeless.

Earlier, I had had lunch with Steve and Michele Kubby. They – along with their two little girls – are being evicted from their home on the Sunshine Coast because their landlady’s fire insurance has been canceled because of the Kubby’s perfectly legal medical cannabis crop.

The Canadian government has encouraged insurance companies to deny fire insurance to homeowners with illegal grow ops, but they forgot to make an exception for people with Health Canada exemptions. So this is just one more example of the failure of HC to make a realistic provision for patients to get medical cannabis. This is terrible for Steve, and he was showing the strain. It is absurd that someone with cancer has to fight to be able live in peace.

Similarly, Da Kine is needed because Health Canada will not – and the Compassion Societies cannot – take care of all of the sick and dying people who need cannabis. Yesterday, The Vancouver Sun reported that “Only about 15% of the 160,000 Canadians who died last year of a terminal ill had access to palliative care.”

The inside headline read, “Many Canadians ‘needlessly dying in pain.’”

The Canadian government insists that it alone is responsible for the health care of Canadians. They have the money to send a small army into Da Kine, because they may be selling medical cannabis to people who won’t die without it, but they don’t have the money to keep many Canadians from “needlessly dying in pain.” That is why Da Kine and the Kubbys must ultimately prevail and cannabis prohibition will fail.

Have the sick and dying liberated us yet?
